idiom_name: interface-preserving delegating component + policy chain + out-of-band control
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define (or reuse) the service contract as the one artifact both sides honour, then implement a component that exposes exactly that contract and forwards every operation to the real service unchanged, with policy applied around the delegation. Keep policies in an ordered chain so new control is a new link rather than an edit to the service, and drive the chain from an out-of-band control source (routes, timeouts, limits, certificates, mirroring rules) instead of compiled code. Decide deliberately where the proxy lives - in-process wrapper, co-located sidecar or shared gateway - because interface equivalence is identical in all three while cost, failure mode and control-plane requirements are not. Whatever the placement, delegation must preserve error taxonomy, deadlines and idempotency semantics.
code_sketch:
contract ServiceApi                      # one artifact both sides honour

proxy ServiceProxy(real: ServiceApi, chain: [Interceptor], config: ControlPlane):
    implements ServiceApi
    on exchange(op):
        ctx = op.context
        chain.before(ctx)                # auth, tracing, limits, routing
        result = real.exchange(op)       # delegate unchanged, same errors
        chain.after(ctx, result)         # metrics, reply routing, redaction
        return result                    # caller still sees ServiceApi
pitfalls: Writing the forwarders by hand instead of generating them from the contract: the proxy drifts and the equivalence guarantee is silently lost.
Letting the proxy change semantics (errors remapped, retries hidden, ordering broken) while claiming transparency; callers must be able to reason about the contract the proxy exposes.
Controlling only in-process traffic: a wrapper inside one client cannot govern other clients, other languages or traffic in the other direction.
Configuring the proxy out of band without observing which configuration version is in effect, so an incident cannot be attributed to a policy rollout.

Wrong move: configuring transparent retries at the proxy while callers also retry -> each layer multiplies attempts against a downstream that is already degraded, and the resulting retry storm converts one slow service into a fleet-wide cascading failure -> instead retry at one deliberately chosen layer, cap attempts, add exponential backoff with jitter, and propagate a deadline so no hop can reset the budget.

Wrong move: assuming an authorization filter configured once protects every path -> Envoy's own ext_authz documentation warns that after a route-cache clear a request can be redirected to an endpoint with different authorization requirements, bypassing the check -> instead make the auth decision consistent across routes, fail closed on authorizer errors, and treat per-route overrides and conditional-invocation settings as reviewed security configuration.

Wrong move: trusting per-hop circuit breakers and local retry budgets in a mesh as system-wide protection -> multi-hop analysis shows locally-capped retries still amplify across deep call graphs, so a proxy that is 'safe' per hop is unsafe in composition -> instead instrument retry rate and amplification across the whole call graph and shed or throttle based on propagated pressure, not just local state.
